title: Ἀντίλοχος ἄγγελος
about: Menelaus leaves the body and searches the line with his eyes like an eagle until he sees Antilochus on the left of the battle. He tells him that a god is rolling woe upon the Danaans, that Patroclus is dead and that Hector has his armour, and sends him running to Achilles with the news. Antilochus, silenced and in tears, hands his armour to Laodocus and goes. Menelaus will not go himself to the Pylians’ part of the line, and sends Thrasymedes there, then returns to Patroclus. He tells the Ajaxes what he has done and asks for a plan to save the body and themselves. Great Ajax agrees: Menelaus and Meriones are to lift the corpse and carry it, while the two Ajaxes face the Trojans behind. The Trojans, with Aeneas and Hector first, rush on like dogs after a wounded boar, but fall back when the Ajaxes turn on them. The bearers hurry to the ships through fighting like a spreading fire, and the Ajaxes hold the Trojans off as a wooded spur turns a flood. The Achaeans stream away like birds before a falcon, and there is no respite from the war.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἀπέβη ξανθὸς Μενέλαος,
πάντοσε παπταίνων ὥς τ’ αἰετός, ὅν ῥά τέ φασιν
ὀξύτατον δέρκεσθαι ὑπουρανίων πετεηνῶν,
sentences.l:
So then, having spoken, went away fair-haired Menelaus,
everywhere glancing about, like an eagle, which they say
is the sharpest at seeing of the winged creatures under heaven,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and fair-haired Menelaus went away, glancing about on every side like an eagle, which they say sees most sharply of all the winged creatures under heaven;
sentences.n: Menelaus has just finished speaking to the Ajaxes and Meriones, and now leaves the body to look for Antilochus. His searching glance is compared to an eagle’s: παπταίνων ‘glancing about’ is the word for a man scanning, and πάντοσε ‘on every side’ goes with it. ὀξύτατον δέρκεσθαι is ‘sharpest at seeing’, with ὑπουρανίων πετεηνῶν ‘of the winged creatures under heaven’ as the group compared. The simile continues in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὅν τε καὶ ὑψόθ’ ἐόντα πόδας ταχὺς οὐκ ἔλαθε πτὼξ
θάμνῳ ὑπ’ ἀμφικόμῳ κατακείμενος, ἀλλά τ’ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ
ἔσσυτο, καί τέ μιν ὦκα λαβὼν ἐξείλετο θυμόν.
sentences.l:
which even high up, being there, the swift-in-feet cowering hare did not escape,
lying under a bush with leaves all round, but at it
it rushed, and quickly, taking it, it took out its life.
sentences.i: Even when it is high up, the hare, swift of foot, lying under a thick-leaved bush, does not escape it, but the eagle swoops down on him, and quickly seizing him takes out his life.
sentences.n: The hare is πτώξ, built on the idea of cowering. ἀμφίκομος is from ἀμφί ‘around’ and κόμη ‘hair, foliage’. The aorists ἔλαθε, ἔσσυτο and ἐξείλετο are used for what the eagle always does, and the English turns them to the present; θυμός here is the life that leaves the body.

sentences.t:
ὣς τότε σοὶ Μενέλαε διοτρεφὲς ὄσσε φαεινὼ
πάντοσε δινείσθην πολέων κατὰ ἔθνος ἑταίρων,
εἴ που Νέστορος υἱὸν ἔτι ζώοντα ἴδοιτο.
sentences.l:
So then for you, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured one, your two eyes, shining,
everywhere were whirled about over the company of your many companions,
if anywhere Nestor’s son still living he might see.
sentences.i: So then, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured one, your two shining eyes turned in every direction over the company of your many companions, in case you might see Nestor’s son still alive.
sentences.n: ὣς τότε answers the simile’s ὥς τ’ αἰετός: ‘so then…’. The poet now speaks to Menelaus directly, σοὶ … Μενέλαε, and διοτρεφές ‘Zeus-nurtured one’ is the stock epithet in the vocative. ὄσσε φαεινώ is a dual, ‘the two shining eyes’, and δινείσθην is the matching dual verb from δινέω ‘whirl’, ‘were whirled about’. κατὰ ἔθνος … ἑταίρων is ‘over the company of companions’. εἴ που … ἴδοιτο is an optative after a past verb, ‘in case he might see’, put into the second person in the English because the poet is speaking to Menelaus. Νέστορος υἱόν is Antilochus, not yet named.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ μάλ’ αἶψ’ ἐνόησε μάχης ἐπ’ ἀριστερὰ πάσης
θαρσύνονθ’ ἑτάρους καὶ ἐποτρύνοντα μάχεσθαι,
ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱστάμενος προσέφη ξανθὸς Μενέλαος·
sentences.l:
And him very quickly he noticed, on the left of all the battle,
cheering his companions and urging them on to fight,
and standing close by he addressed him, fair-haired Menelaus:
sentences.i: And he very soon noticed him on the left of the whole battle, cheering his companions and urging them on to fight; and, standing close beside him, fair-haired Menelaus spoke to him:
sentences.n: The first two lines recur elsewhere in the Iliad, and the third is the formula for a man who comes up close and speaks. ἐνόησε is the aorist of νοέω ‘notice’, and μάχης ἐπ’ ἀριστερά is ‘on the left of the battle’. θαρσύνοντα ‘cheering’ and ἐποτρύνοντα ‘urging on’ describe Antilochus. ἀγχοῦ … ἱστάμενος is ‘standing close by’, and προσέφη is ‘addressed’. Menelaus’ speech follows at once.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίλοχ’ εἰ δ’ ἄγε δεῦρο διοτρεφὲς ὄφρα πύθηαι
λυγρῆς ἀγγελίης, ἣ μὴ ὤφελλε γενέσθαι.
sentences.l:
“Antilochus, come now, here, Zeus-nurtured one, so that you may learn
of grievous news, which ought not to have happened.
sentences.i: “Antilochus, come here now, Zeus-nurtured one, so that you may learn of grievous news, news that ought never to have happened.
sentences.n: Menelaus speaks to Antilochus, using διοτρεφές, the same ‘Zeus-nurtured one’ epithet the poet used of Menelaus himself. εἰ δ’ ἄγε is ‘come now’, a phrase of urging, and δεῦρο is ‘here’. ὄφρα πύθηαι is a purpose clause, ‘so that you may learn’, with πυνθάνομαι taking the genitive λυγρῆς ἀγγελίης ‘grievous news’. ἣ μὴ ὤφελλε γενέσθαι is a relative clause, ‘which ought not to have happened’: ὤφελλε with an infinitive says what should have been and was not.

sentences.t:
ἤδη μὲν σὲ καὶ αὐτὸν ὀΐομαι εἰσορόωντα
γιγνώσκειν ὅτι πῆμα θεὸς Δαναοῖσι κυλίνδει,
νίκη δὲ Τρώων·
sentences.i: I think that you yourself, looking on, already know that a god is rolling woe upon the Danaans, and that victory belongs to the Trojans;
sentences.n: ὀΐομαι ‘I think’ governs the infinitive γιγνώσκειν ‘to know’, with σέ as its subject and εἰσορόωντα ‘looking on’ agreeing with it. καὶ αὐτόν is ‘you yourself’, who have seen it with your own eyes. πῆμα is ‘woe’, and κυλίνδει ‘rolls’ pictures it as something rolled upon the Danaans; θεός is an unnamed god, understood to be Zeus. In νίκη δὲ Τρώων the verb ‘is’ is understood, ‘the victory is the Trojans’’. Δαναοῖσι is ‘Danaans’, one of the poem’s three names for the army.

sentences.t:
πέφαται δ’ ὤριστος Ἀχαιῶν
Πάτροκλος, μεγάλη δὲ ποθὴ Δαναοῖσι τέτυκται.
sentences.l:
and has been killed the best of the Achaeans,
Patroclus, and a great lack for the Danaans has been made.
sentences.i: and the best of the Achaeans, Patroclus, has been killed, and a great lack has come upon the Danaans.
sentences.n: πέφαται is the perfect passive of the verb for ‘kill’, ‘has been killed’, and ὤριστος is ὁ ἄριστος run together by crasis, ‘the best’. ποθή is ‘lack’, the felt want of a man who is gone. τέτυκται is the perfect passive of τεύχω ‘make’, ‘has been made’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σύ γ’ αἶψ’ Ἀχιλῆϊ θέων ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν
εἰπεῖν, αἴ κε τάχιστα νέκυν ἐπὶ νῆα σαώσῃ
γυμνόν·
sentences.i: But you, run quickly to Achilles at the ships of the Achaeans and tell him, in case he can bring the corpse safe to a ship as fast as he can, naked as it is;
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ σύ γ’ is ‘but you at least’. θέων ‘running’ goes with σύ, and εἰπεῖν is an infinitive used as a command, ‘tell’. αἴ κε τάχιστα … σαώσῃ is ‘in case he might bring safe as quickly as possible’, with the subjunctive after αἴ κε; the object is νέκυν, and ἐπὶ νῆα is ‘to a ship’. γυμνόν ‘naked’ means stripped of its armour, and it opens line 693, held over from the clause before, which stresses it.

sentences.t: ἀτὰρ τά γε τεύχε’ ἔχει κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ.
sentences.l: but the armour, that, has Hector of the glancing helmet.”
sentences.i: but Hector of the glancing helmet has the armour.”
sentences.n: ἀτάρ ‘but’ sets the stripped body against the armour. τά γε … τεύχε’ is ‘those arms’, with τεύχε’ the elided τεύχεα ‘armour’, which Hector took from Patroclus. κορυθαίολος is the stock epithet of Hector, ‘of the glancing helmet’: κόρυς ‘helmet’ and αἰόλος ‘quick-moving, glancing’. This ends Menelaus’ speech.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, Ἀντίλοχος δὲ κατέστυγε μῦθον ἀκούσας·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and Antilochus was horror-struck, having heard the word;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Antilochus was appalled to hear what he said;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ closes the speech. κατέστυγε is the aorist of καταστυγέω, ‘was struck with horror’, and μῦθον ἀκούσας is ‘having heard the word’, the news Menelaus gave. A new paragraph begins here, as Antilochus reacts.

sentences.t:
δὴν δέ μιν ἀμφασίη ἐπέων λάβε, τὼ δέ οἱ ὄσσε
δακρυόφι πλῆσθεν, θαλερὴ δέ οἱ ἔσχετο φωνή.
sentences.l:
and for a long time speechlessness of words took hold of him, and his two eyes
were filled with tears, and his full voice was checked.
sentences.i: And for a long time speechlessness took hold of him, and his eyes filled with tears, and his strong voice was choked.
sentences.n: δὴν is ‘for a long time’, and ἀμφασίη is ‘speechlessness’, a noun made from the root of the verb ‘say’ with the negative prefix; ἐπέων ‘of words’ tells what he is without. The second line is a stock line: the Odyssey has it for a woman, and the Iliad here gives it to a man, so only the sense of the pronoun οἱ changes (‘his’). πλῆσθεν is the aorist passive ‘were filled’, plural in form although its subject ὄσσε is a dual, ‘the two eyes’, and θαλερή ‘full’ is a word that in other places is ‘abundant’ of tears; ἔσχετο is ‘was checked’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὧς Μενελάου ἐφημοσύνης ἀμέλησε,
βῆ δὲ θέειν, τὰ δὲ τεύχε’ ἀμύμονι δῶκεν ἑταίρῳ
Λαοδόκῳ, ὅς οἱ σχεδὸν ἔστρεφε μώνυχας ἵππους.
sentences.l:
But not even so of Menelaus’ behest was he neglectful,
and he went to run, and the armour to a blameless companion he gave,
to Laodocus, who near him was turning the solid-hoofed horses.
sentences.i: But even so he did not neglect Menelaus’ behest, and he set off running, and gave his armour to his blameless companion Laodocus, who was turning the solid-hoofed horses about near him.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ὧς is ‘not even so’, in spite of his grief. ἐφημοσύνης is a rare word for an order laid on someone, here ‘behest’, and ἀμέλησε ‘neglected’ takes the genitive. βῆ δὲ θέειν is the epic way of beginning an action, ‘set off running’. τὰ … τεύχε’ is ‘his armour’, left behind, it seems, so that he can run lightly. ἀμύμονι is the stock ‘blameless’. Λαοδόκῳ is Laodocus, a companion who is minding Antilochus’ horses; μώνυχας ἵππους is ‘solid-hoofed horses’.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν δάκρυ χέοντα πόδες φέρον ἐκ πολέμοιο
Πηλεΐδῃ Ἀχιλῆϊ κακὸν ἔπος ἀγγελέοντα.
sentences.l:
Him, a tear shedding, his feet carried out of the war
to Peleus’-son Achilles, an evil word about to tell.
sentences.i: His feet carried him, shedding tears, out of the war to Peleus’ son Achilles, to tell him an evil word.
sentences.n: A new paragraph, after the break: the scene follows Antilochus. τὸν μὲν has μέν without a following δέ at once; the contrast comes at 702–706, where Menelaus is described. δάκρυ χέοντα is ‘shedding tears’, and πόδες φέρον ‘his feet carried’ is a quick way of saying he ran. ἀγγελέοντα is a future participle, ‘about to tell’, and κακὸν ἔπος is ‘an evil word’. Πηλεΐδῃ Ἀχιλῆϊ is ‘Peleus’ son Achilles’, with the patronymic.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρα σοὶ Μενέλαε διοτρεφὲς ἤθελε θυμὸς
τειρομένοις ἑτάροισιν ἀμυνέμεν, ἔνθεν ἀπῆλθεν
Ἀντίλοχος, μεγάλη δὲ ποθὴ Πυλίοισιν ἐτύχθη·
sentences.i: Nor was your heart, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured one, willing to defend the worn-down companions at the place Antilochus had left, and the Pylians were left with a great lack;
sentences.n: The poet addresses Menelaus again, as at 679. The sentence has to be read with the next: Menelaus’ heart was not willing to go and defend the Pylians’ part of the line, so he sent Thrasymedes instead. ἀμυνέμεν is the infinitive of ἀμύνω, which with a dative of the person and no thing warded off is ‘defend’, and τειρομένοις is ‘worn down’. ἔνθεν ἀπῆλθεν Ἀντίλοχος is ‘from where Antilochus went away’, the place where the Pylians were fighting. ποθή is ‘lack’, as at 690, and ἐτύχθη the aorist passive of τεύχω ‘make’. Πυλίοισιν is ‘for the Pylians’, Nestor’s men.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅ γε τοῖσιν μὲν Θρασυμήδεα δῖον ἀνῆκεν,
αὐτὸς δ’ αὖτ’ ἐπὶ Πατρόκλῳ ἥρωϊ βεβήκει,
στῆ δὲ παρ’ Αἰάντεσσι θέων, εἶθαρ δὲ προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
but he to them, Thrasymedes, heavenly, sent up,
and himself again over Patroclus the hero had gone,
and stood beside the Ajaxes, running, and at once spoke to them:
sentences.i: But to them he sent heavenly Thrasymedes, and went back to stand over the hero Patroclus himself, and he ran and stood beside the Ajaxes and at once spoke to them:
sentences.n: ἀλλά sets what Menelaus did against what he would not do. ἀνῆκεν is the aorist of ἀνίημι ‘send up’, and Θρασυμήδεα δῖον is ‘heavenly Thrasymedes’, the other son of Nestor. βεβήκει is the pluperfect of βαίνω, ‘had gone’ and so ‘was standing’, and αὐτὸς δ’ αὖτ’ is ‘and he himself again, in turn’. Πατρόκλῳ ἥρωϊ is ‘Patroclus the hero’. Αἰάντεσσι is the dative plural ‘Ajaxes’, as at 17.668, and εἶθαρ is ‘at once’.

sentences.t:
κεῖνον μὲν δὴ νηυσὶν ἐπιπροέηκα θοῇσιν
ἐλθεῖν εἰς Ἀχιλῆα πόδας ταχύν·
sentences.l:
“That man indeed I have sent forth, to the swift ships,
to go to Achilles, swift in feet;
sentences.i: “As for him, I have sent him off to the swift ships, to go to Achilles, swift of foot;
sentences.n: Menelaus speaks to the Ajaxes. κεῖνον is Antilochus, ‘that man’, and ἐπιπροέηκα is the aorist of a verb meaning ‘send forth towards’. θοῇσιν is the stock ‘swift’ of ships. πόδας ταχύν is ‘swift in feet’, an accusative of respect, as in the standing πόδας ὠκύς.
sentences.mark: Menelaus tells the Ajaxes his plan

sentences.t:
οὐδέ μιν οἴω
νῦν ἰέναι μάλα περ κεχολωμένον Ἕκτορι δίῳ·
sentences.l:
and not him, I think,
now to go, though very much angered with heavenly Hector;
sentences.i: and I do not think he will go now, however angry he is with heavenly Hector;
sentences.n: οὐδέ μιν οἴω νῦν ἰέναι is ‘and I do not think he will go now’, the negative standing with ὀΐω though it belongs in sense to the infinitive; ὀΐω is ‘think’, and ἰέναι the infinitive of εἶμι ‘go’. μάλα περ κεχολωμένον is ‘though very much angered’, a perfect participle of χολόω from χόλος ‘anger’. The anger is Achilles’, against Hector for killing Patroclus. Ἕκτορι δίῳ is ‘heavenly Hector’.

sentences.t: οὐ γάρ πως ἂν γυμνὸς ἐὼν Τρώεσσι μάχοιτο.
sentences.l: for in no way could he, being naked, fight the Trojans.
sentences.i: for there is no way he could fight the Trojans without his armour.
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ πως ἄν … μάχοιτο is a potential optative, ‘in no way could he fight’, and the reason for the line before: Achilles has no armour. γυμνὸς ἐών is ‘being naked’, which here means unarmed, since Hector took Achilles’ armour with Patroclus’ body. Τρώεσσι is the dative after μάχοιτο.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δ’ αὐτοί περ φραζώμεθα μῆτιν ἀρίστην,
ἠμὲν ὅπως τὸν νεκρὸν ἐρύσσομεν, ἠδὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ
Τρώων ἐξ ἐνοπῆς θάνατον καὶ κῆρα φύγωμεν.
sentences.l:
But we ourselves, let us plan the best cunning,
both how the corpse we may drag, and also ourselves
from the Trojans’ shouting death and the death-fate may escape.”
sentences.i: But let us ourselves plan the best stroke of cunning: both how we may drag the corpse away, and how we ourselves may escape death and the spirit of death out of the Trojans’ shouting.”
sentences.n: The lines are close to Ajax’s words at 17.634–635 in the preceding part, with ‘but we’ (ἡμεῖς δ’) in place of ‘but come’ (ἀλλ’ ἄγετ’) and a different end. φραζώμεθα is a subjunctive of urging, ‘let us plan’, with μῆτιν ἀρίστην ‘the best cunning’. ἠμὲν ὅπως … ἠδὲ καὶ is ‘both how … and also how’, and ἐρύσσομεν and φύγωμεν are subjunctives in the indirect question. ἐνοπῆς is ‘shouting’; Τρώων ἐξ ἐνοπῆς is ‘out of the Trojans’ shouting’. θάνατον καὶ κῆρα is ‘death and the spirit of death’, the κήρ that is not the same word as κῆρ ‘heart’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα μέγας Τελαμώνιος Αἴας·
sentences.l: Him then answered great Telamonian Ajax:
sentences.i: Then great Telamonian Ajax answered him:
sentences.n: The whole-line formula that introduces a reply: ἠμείβετο is ‘answered’, and the epithet Τελαμώνιος tells the greater Ajax from the lesser. The same line stands elsewhere in the Iliad; at 17.628 in the preceding part Ajax is introduced by a related line, τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχε μέγας Τελαμώνιος Αἴας.

sentences.t: πάντα κατ’ αἶσαν ἔειπες ἀγακλεὲς ὦ Μενέλαε·
sentences.l: “Everything in due measure you have said, very famous Menelaus;
sentences.i: “You have said everything as was fitting, very famous Menelaus;
sentences.n: Ajax’s reply opens with praise. κατ’ αἶσαν is ‘in due measure’, ἔειπες the aorist of a verb ‘say’, and ἀγακλεές the vocative of ἀγακλεής ‘very famous’, ἀγα- being an intensifier. ὦ Μενέλαε closes the address.
sentences.mark: Ajax agrees and shares out the work

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ μὲν καὶ Μηριόνης ὑποδύντε μάλ’ ὦκα
νεκρὸν ἀείραντες φέρετ’ ἐκ πόνου·
sentences.l:
but you and Meriones, getting under it very quickly,
the corpse having lifted, carry out of the toil;
sentences.i: but you and Meriones, getting under it very quickly, lift the corpse and carry it out of the toil;
sentences.n: ὑποδύντε is a dual aorist participle, ‘the two of you having got under’ the body, with σύ and Μηριόνης as the pair. ἀείραντες ‘having lifted’ is plural in form, although two men are meant. φέρετ’ is an imperative, ‘carry’. ἐκ πόνου is ‘out of the toil’, meaning the fighting.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὄπισθε
νῶϊ μαχησόμεθα Τρωσίν τε καὶ Ἕκτορι δίῳ
ἶσον θυμὸν ἔχοντες ὁμώνυμοι, οἳ τὸ πάρος περ
μίμνομεν ὀξὺν Ἄρηα παρ’ ἀλλήλοισι μένοντες.
sentences.l:
but behind
we two will fight the Trojans and heavenly Hector,
having an equal heart, of the same name, we who even before
have stood against sharp Ares, staying beside one another.”
sentences.i: but behind you we two will fight the Trojans and heavenly Hector, of one equal spirit and bearing one name, we who even before this have stood against keen battle, staying side by side.”
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’, and ὄπισθε ‘behind’, mean behind those who carry the body. νῶϊ is the dual ‘we two’, Ajax son of Telamon and Ajax son of Oileus. ἶσον θυμὸν ἔχοντες is ‘having an equal heart’, and ὁμώνυμοι ‘of the same name’ says both are called Ajax. οἳ … μίμνομεν is ‘we who wait for, withstand’, with ὀξὺν Ἄρηα ‘keen battle’, Ares standing for war. παρ’ ἀλλήλοισι μένοντες is ‘staying beside one another’. This ends Ajax’s speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα νεκρὸν ἀπὸ χθονὸς ἀγκάζοντο
ὕψι μάλα μεγάλως·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they the corpse from the ground took up in their arms,
very high, mightily;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they gathered the corpse up in their arms from the ground, very high, with a mighty heave;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. ὣς ἔφαθ’ closes the speech. οἳ δ’ are Menelaus and Meriones, the two who were told to lift. ἀγκάζοντο is from ἀγκάζομαι ‘take in the arms’ (ἀγκάς ‘in the arms’), and ὕψι μάλα μεγάλως is ‘very high, mightily’, the lifting of a heavy dead man from the ground.

sentences.t:
ἐπὶ δ’ ἴαχε λαὸς ὄπισθε
Τρωϊκός, ὡς εἴδοντο νέκυν αἴροντας Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.l:
and cried out loudly behind them the people
of the Trojans, when they saw the Achaeans lifting the corpse.
sentences.i: and behind them the Trojan host raised a loud cry when they saw the Achaeans lifting the corpse.
sentences.n: ἐπὶ … ἴαχε is a verb with its prefix separated (tmesis), ‘cried out at it’, and ἴαχε is ‘cried out loudly’. λαὸς … Τρωϊκός is ‘the Trojan people’, the whole Trojan army. ὡς εἴδοντο is ‘when they saw’, from the middle of the verb ‘see’, and νέκυν αἴροντας ‘lifting the corpse’ shows what the Trojans are crying out against.

sentences.t:
ἴθυσαν δὲ κύνεσσιν ἐοικότες, οἵ τ’ ἐπὶ κάπρῳ
βλημένῳ ἀΐξωσι πρὸ κούρων θηρητήρων·
sentences.l:
And they charged straight, like dogs, which upon a boar
struck dart before young hunters;
sentences.i: And they charged straight on, like dogs that dart at a struck boar ahead of the young hunters;
sentences.n: ἴθυσαν is the aorist of ἰθύω ‘charge straight’, and κύνεσσιν ἐοικότες is ‘like dogs’. The simile begins; οἵ τ’ … ἀΐξωσι is a subjunctive in a general statement, ‘which dart’. βλημένῳ is an aorist participle of βάλλω ‘strike’, middle in form and passive in sense, here ‘a boar that has been struck’, and κούρων θηρητήρων is ‘young hunters’.

sentences.t:
ἕως μὲν γάρ τε θέουσι διαρραῖσαι μεμαῶτες,
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἐν τοῖσιν ἑλίξεται ἀλκὶ πεποιθώς,
ἄψ τ’ ἀνεχώρησαν διά τ’ ἔτρεσαν ἄλλυδις ἄλλος.
sentences.i: for as long as they run, eager to tear it apart; but when it wheels round among them, trusting in its strength, they draw back and scatter in fright, one this way and one that.
sentences.n: The simile goes on. ἕως μὲν … ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή sets two moments against each other, ‘for as long as … but when’. διαρραῖσαι is ‘to tear apart’, and μεμαῶτες is ‘eager’. ἑλίξεται is an aorist subjunctive from ἑλίσσω ‘turn about’, and ἀλκὶ πεποιθώς is ‘trusting in its might’. ἄψ τ’ ἀνεχώρησαν and διά τ’ ἔτρεσαν are aorists of what always happens, with διά ‘apart’ separated from ἔτρεσαν ‘took fright’. ἄλλυδις ἄλλος is ‘one this way, one that’.

sentences.t:
ὣς Τρῶες εἷος μὲν ὁμιλαδὸν αἰὲν ἕποντο
νύσσοντες ξίφεσίν τε καὶ ἔγχεσιν ἀμφιγύοισιν·
sentences.l:
So the Trojans, for as long as in a throng ever they followed,
stabbing with swords and with double-pointed spears;
sentences.i: So the Trojans, for as long as they kept following in a throng, stabbed with swords and double-pointed spears;
sentences.n: ὣς answers the simile: the Trojans are the dogs. εἷος μέν is ‘for as long as’, a form of ἕως, and the next unit supplies the ἀλλ’ ὅτε ‘but when’ that balances it. ὁμιλαδόν is ‘in a throng’, and ἕποντο is ‘followed’. The line νύσσοντες … ἀμφιγύοισιν recurs elsewhere in the Iliad; ἀμφιγύοισιν is ‘double-pointed’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ Αἴαντε μεταστρεφθέντε κατ’ αὐτοὺς
σταίησαν, τῶν δὲ τράπετο χρώς, οὐδέ τις ἔτλη
πρόσσω ἀΐξας περὶ νεκροῦ δηριάασθαι.
sentences.l:
but when the two Ajaxes, having turned about against them,
stood, of them the skin turned, nor did anyone bring himself
forward darting to fight about the corpse.
sentences.i: but whenever the two Ajaxes turned round to face them and stood their ground, the colour in the Trojans’ skin changed, and no one could bring himself to dart forward and go on fighting over the corpse.
sentences.n: Αἴαντε is a dual, ‘the two Ajaxes’, and μεταστρεφθέντε ‘having turned about’ is a dual participle; κατ’ αὐτούς is ‘against them’. σταίησαν is an optative of repeated action, ‘whenever they stood’. τράπετο χρώς is ‘the skin turned’, that is, the colour left it, from fear. οὐδέ τις ἔτλη, with an infinitive, is ‘no one could bring himself’, and πρόσσω ἀΐξας ‘darting forward’ goes with δηριάασθαι ‘fight on’.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἵ γ’ ἐμμεμαῶτε νέκυν φέρον ἐκ πολέμοιο
νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς·
sentences.l:
So they two, eager, the corpse carried out of the war
to the hollow ships;
sentences.i: So the two of them, full of eagerness, carried the corpse out of the war to the hollow ships;
sentences.n: A new paragraph returns to the two carriers. οἵ γ’ is plural in form, but the dual participle ἐμμεμαῶτε shows it means ‘the two of them’, Menelaus and Meriones; ἐμμεμαῶτε is the dual perfect participle of ἐμμαίομαι, ‘eager’. νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς is ‘to the hollow ships’, with the preposition ἔπι after its noun.

sentences.t:
ἐπὶ δὲ πτόλεμος τέτατό σφιν
ἄγριος ἠΰτε πῦρ, τό τ’ ἐπεσσύμενον πόλιν ἀνδρῶν
ὄρμενον ἐξαίφνης φλεγέθει, μινύθουσι δὲ οἶκοι
ἐν σέλαϊ μεγάλῳ·
sentences.l:
and upon them war was stretched
savage like fire, which, rushing upon a city of men,
rising suddenly, blazes, and the houses dwindle away
in a great blaze;
sentences.i: and the war was stretched out over them, savage as fire, which rushes on a city of men, springs up suddenly and blazes, and the houses dwindle away in a great blaze;
sentences.n: ἐπὶ … τέτατο, with the preposition separated, is ‘was stretched upon’; τέτατο is the pluperfect passive of τείνω ‘stretch’. πτόλεμος is an older spelling of πόλεμος ‘war’, and ἄγριος is ‘savage’. ἠΰτε is ‘like’, starting a fire simile. ἐπεσσύμενον and ὄρμενον are participles, ‘rushing on’ and ‘rising’, with ἐξαίφνης ‘suddenly’. φλεγέθει is ‘blazes’, and μινύθουσι is ‘dwindle away’, of the houses burning. σέλαϊ is the dative of σέλας ‘blaze’.

sentences.t: τὸ δ’ ἐπιβρέμει ἲς ἀνέμοιο.
sentences.l: and upon it roars the force of the wind.
sentences.i: and the force of the wind roars upon it.
sentences.n: τό is ‘it’, the fire. ἐπιβρέμει is ‘roars upon’, from ἐπιβρέμω, and ἲς ἀνέμοιο is ‘the force of the wind’; ἲς is ‘force’. The wind feeds the blaze.

sentences.t:
ὣς μὲν τοῖς ἵππων τε καὶ ἀνδρῶν αἰχμητάων
ἀζηχὴς ὀρυμαγδὸς ἐπήϊεν ἐρχομένοισιν·
sentences.l:
So for them of horses and of men, spearmen,
incessant din came upon them as they went;
sentences.i: So, as they went, an incessant din of horses and of spearmen came upon them;
sentences.n: ὣς μὲν τοῖς answers the fire: ‘so for them’. ἵππων τε καὶ ἀνδρῶν αἰχμητάων is ‘of horses and of men, spearmen’, the noise made by the pursuers. ἀζηχής ‘incessant’ and ὀρυμαγδός ‘din’ are one phrase, and ἐπήϊεν is ‘came upon’, the imperfect of ἔπειμι. The dative ἐρχομένοισιν is ‘for them as they went’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὥς θ’ ἡμίονοι κρατερὸν μένος ἀμφιβαλόντες
ἕλκωσ’ ἐξ ὄρεος κατὰ παιπαλόεσσαν ἀταρπὸν
ἢ δοκὸν ἠὲ δόρυ μέγα νήϊον·
sentences.i: And they were like mules, which have cast strong might about themselves and drag down a rugged footpath from the mountain either a beam or a great timber for a ship;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ are the two carriers, compared now to mules. κρατερὸν μένος ἀμφιβαλόντες is ‘having cast strong might about them’, as one puts on a garment. ἕλκωσι is a subjunctive in a general statement, ‘drag’. ἀταρπός is a ‘footpath’, παιπαλόεσσαν ‘rugged’. δοκός is ‘a beam’, and δόρυ is wood, ‘a timber’; νήϊον ‘for a ship’ is an adjective with it.

sentences.t:
ἐν δέ τε θυμὸς
τείρεθ’ ὁμοῦ καμάτῳ τε καὶ ἱδρῷ σπευδόντεσσιν·
sentences.l:
and in them the heart is worn down
together with weariness and sweat, for them hurrying;
sentences.i: and the heart in them is worn down by weariness and sweat together as they hurry;
sentences.n: ἐν δέ τε is ‘and in them’, with θυμός ‘heart’ as the subject of τείρεθ’, ‘is worn down’. ὁμοῦ is ‘together’, going with ‘weariness and sweat’, and καμάτῳ τε καὶ ἱδρῷ is ‘weariness and sweat’. σπευδόντεσσιν is a dative plural participle, ‘for those hurrying’.

sentences.t: ὣς οἵ γ’ ἐμμεμαῶτε νέκυν φέρον.
sentences.l: So they two, eager, the corpse carried.
sentences.i: So the two of them, full of eagerness, carried the corpse.
sentences.n: The line returns to the point of the mule simile and repeats 735 without the rest of the verse: οἵ γ’ is plural in form but means ‘the two of them’, as the dual ἐμμεμαῶτε ‘eager’ shows; φέρον is ‘carried’. The stop falls in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὄπισθεν
Αἴαντ’ ἰσχανέτην, ὥς τε πρὼν ἰσχάνει ὕδωρ
ὑλήεις πεδίοιο διαπρύσιον τετυχηκώς,
sentences.l:
But behind
the two Ajaxes held back, as a spur holds back water,
wooded, right across the plain having come to be,
sentences.i: But behind them the two Ajaxes held the Trojans back, as a wooded spur holds back water, a spur lying right across the plain,
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὄπισθεν ‘but behind’ is the other side of the picture: the two carry, the Ajaxes hold off the pursuit. Αἴαντ’ ἰσχανέτην is a dual, ‘the two Ajaxes held back’, from ἰσχάνω ‘hold back’. πρών is ‘spur’, ὕδωρ ‘water’, ὑλήεις ‘wooded’. διαπρύσιον πεδίοιο is ‘right through the plain’, and τετυχηκώς, a perfect participle of τυγχάνω, is taken as ‘lying’, but its exact shade is not certain. The Ajaxes’ object, the Trojans, is not named.

sentences.t:
ὅς τε καὶ ἰφθίμων ποταμῶν ἀλεγεινὰ ῥέεθρα
ἴσχει, ἄφαρ δέ τε πᾶσι ῥόον πεδίον δὲ τίθησι
πλάζων·
sentences.i: a spur that checks even the grievous streams of mighty rivers, and at once turns the current of all of them out over the plain, making them stray;
sentences.n: ὅς τε καὶ continues the simile: ‘which even’. ἴσχει is ‘checks’, a form of the verb ἰσχάνει ‘holds back’ used just before. ἰφθίμων ποταμῶν is ‘of mighty rivers’, and ἀλεγεινὰ ῥέεθρα ‘grievous streams’. ῥόον πεδίον δὲ τίθησι is ‘sets the current toward the plain’, and πλάζων ‘making stray’ says the water is turned off its course; the object is the current, and the English gives the plural for ‘all’.

sentences.t: οὐδέ τί μιν σθένεϊ ῥηγνῦσι ῥέοντες·
sentences.l: and not at all it with strength do they break, flowing;
sentences.i: and for all their flowing, they do not break it with their strength;
sentences.n: μιν is the spur, and ῥηγνῦσι is ‘they break’, from ῥήγνυμι. σθένεϊ is ‘with strength’, the strength of the rivers, and ῥέοντες ‘flowing’ gives the sense ‘though they flow’. The rivers cannot burst the spur, as the Trojans cannot burst the Ajaxes.

sentences.t:
ὣς αἰεὶ Αἴαντε μάχην ἀνέεργον ὀπίσσω
Τρώων·
sentences.l:
So always the two Ajaxes held back the battle behind
of the Trojans;
sentences.i: So the two Ajaxes always held back the Trojan fighting from behind;
sentences.n: ὣς closes the spur simile. ἀνέεργον is the imperfect of ἀνείργω ‘hold back’, and ὀπίσσω … Τρώων is ‘behind, the Trojans’ battle’, the fighting of the Trojans coming from the rear of the carriers. Αἴαντε is again a dual. ὀπίσσω could instead be taken with ἀνέεργον as ‘back’; the English takes it as ‘from behind’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἅμ’ ἕποντο, δύω δ’ ἐν τοῖσι μάλιστα
Αἰνείας τ’ Ἀγχισιάδης καὶ φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ.
sentences.l:
and they together followed, and two among them most of all,
Aeneas, Anchises’-son, and glorious Hector.
sentences.i: and the Trojans pressed after them together, and two among them most of all: Aeneas, son of Anchises, and glorious Hector.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ are the Trojans, who ἅμ’ ἕποντο ‘followed together’. δύω δ’ … μάλιστα is ‘and two most of all’. Αἰνείας is Aeneas, and Ἀγχισιάδης is ‘son of Anchises’, a patronymic. φαίδιμος is the stock epithet of Hector, ‘glorious’.

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’ ὥς τε ψαρῶν νέφος ἔρχεται ἠὲ κολοιῶν
οὖλον κεκλήγοντες, ὅτε προΐδωσιν ἰόντα
κίρκον, ὅ τε σμικρῇσι φόνον φέρει ὀρνίθεσσιν,
sentences.l:
And of them, as a cloud of starlings goes, or of jackdaws,
ruinously shrieking, when they see beforehand coming
a falcon, which to small birds slaughter brings,
sentences.i: And like a cloud of starlings or of jackdaws they go, shrieking ruinously when they catch sight of a falcon coming, a bird that brings slaughter to small birds,
sentences.n: A last simile. τῶν δ’ is ‘and of them’, the Achaeans, but the genitive is hard to place, and the English turns it to ‘they’, as the comparison needs a subject. ψαρῶν ‘starlings’ and κολοιῶν ‘jackdaws’ are in the genitive after νέφος ‘cloud’. οὖλον κεκλήγοντες is ‘shrieking’ with an adverb οὖλον taken as ‘ruinously’, from οὖλος; the sense here, deadly or wild, is not certain. προΐδωσιν is ‘see beforehand, catch sight of’. κίρκον is ‘falcon’, φόνον ‘slaughter’, and σμικρῇσι ὀρνίθεσσιν ‘to small birds’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ὑπ’ Αἰνείᾳ τε καὶ Ἕκτορι κοῦροι Ἀχαιῶν
οὖλον κεκλήγοντες ἴσαν, λήθοντο δὲ χάρμης.
sentences.l:
so then before Aeneas and Hector the young men of the Achaeans
ruinously shrieking went, and forgot the joy of battle.
sentences.i: so before Aeneas and Hector the young men of the Achaeans went, shrieking ruinously, and forgot the joy of battle.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρ’ gives the other side of the comparison. ὑπ’ Αἰνείᾳ τε καὶ Ἕκτορι is ‘before Aeneas and Hector’, with ὑπό and the dative meaning ‘under the attack of’. κοῦροι Ἀχαιῶν is ‘young men of the Achaeans’. οὖλον κεκλήγοντες is repeated from the simile. ἴσαν is ‘went’, an imperfect of εἶμι, and λήθοντο … χάρμης is ‘forgot the joy of battle’, with λήθομαι taking the genitive.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δὲ τεύχεα καλὰ πέσον περί τ’ ἀμφί τε τάφρον
φευγόντων Δαναῶν·
sentences.l:
And many arms, fine, fell around and about the ditch
of the Danaans fleeing;
sentences.i: And much fine armour fell round and about the ditch as the Danaans fled;
sentences.n: πολλὰ … τεύχεα καλά is ‘much fine armour’, dropped by the fugitives. πέσον is ‘fell’, and περί τ’ ἀμφί τε is ‘round and about’, two prepositions used as adverbs together. τάφρον is the ditch dug before the Achaean ships, and φευγόντων Δαναῶν is a genitive absolute, ‘as the Danaans were fleeing’.

sentences.t: πολέμου δ’ οὐ γίγνετ’ ἐρωή.
sentences.l: and of the war there is no respite.
sentences.i: and there is no respite from the war.
sentences.n: γίγνετ’ is ‘comes to be’, used here for ‘there is’. ἐρωή is a word with two senses in the poem: ‘rush’ of a missile and ‘respite, drawing back’. The second sense is plainly meant here with πολέμου, and the English gives it as ‘respite’. The part ends with the fighting at the ditch not stopping.
